title: Breaking the SFT Plateau: Multimodal Structured Reinforcement Learning for Chart-to-Code Generation
one_liner: When training a model to turn charts into code, adding more data eventually stops helping, but pairing textual code-correctness checks with visual chart-shape checks breaks through that wall.
lead: Imagine teaching a student to copy a chart into working Python code. At first, more examples help a lot, because the student is still discovering the main rules: how to structure code, where to read data, how to map colors to the chart. But after thousands of examples, the student stops improving even with new data; this is the SFT plateau, where the model has learned the easy patterns and just repeats them. A new paper shows a way to break through it: use two kinds of feedback at once. One judge checks if the code is syntactically correct and pulls the right values from the chart. Another judge renders the code and compares the output picture to the original chart. Together, these two feedback sources wake up the model in ways that more data alone cannot.

paras: Chart-to-code is hard. You have a colorful chart: bars, lines, scatter points, maybe dozens of data series stacked together. You need to write code that recreates it. The model must understand the numbers inside the chart, the colors, the labels, and turn all that into working Python.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the straightforward approach: give the model thousands of chart-code pairs, and it learns to copy the pattern. It works, at first. But experiments show it hits a performance plateau: after a few million training examples, adding more examples barely helps, because the model has already learned the most common patterns and simply repeats them; rare variations do not appear in enough data to sink in. The curve flattens. The model seems stuck.

callout.html: MSRL splits the feedback: one checker verifies the code works and reads the data correctly, while another checker looks at the rendered picture and grades how well it matches the original chart.

steps.text: Train the model using feedback that grades code syntax, rule compliance, and whether extracted values match the chart data.
Continue training with a second judge that renders the code and compares the rendered picture pixel-by-pixel to the original.
Do text-only training first until it converges, then layer in the visual judge; reversing this order weakens the gain.
Use only high-quality training examples (real charts from arXiv papers + code generated by strong models), filtered to avoid noise.
The model breaks through the SFT plateau and reaches new performance levels on standard benchmarks.

paras: The method changes the feedback signal during training. Instead of using only one kind of loss (the distance between predicted code and ground-truth code), it switches to two-sided grading during reinforcement learning: a textual judge that checks code correctness, and a visual judge that checks picture likeness.
object.object: feedback signal: from one kind to two kinds

hidden.name: visual-semantic gap
paras: SFT only measures one thing: whether the model's code matches the ground-truth code string. But two different code strings can render the same picture (different variable names, different loop structures, equivalent operations). The paper names a hidden quantity: structural alignment, measured as how close the rendered output picture looks to the target. This is invisible to text-only training but absolutely needed for real correctness.

The paper estimates it using a visual reward model: a separate trained model that compares two rendered charts and scores how similar they are. A high visual score means the code creates the intended picture, regardless of the exact code string.

heat.caption: Darker means higher visual-semantic alignment (rendered picture closely matches the target chart).

reads.html: The model's hidden problem: it can write code strings that sound right but render wrong pictures. Adding more code examples does not teach it to render correctly because the text-only loss ignores how the picture looks.

The paper introduces a visual reward as a model-based evaluator that scores structural similarity between the rendered code output and the ground-truth chart. This reveals whether the model is learning to produce visually correct outputs, not just syntactically valid code.

mechanism.h2: Why two judges wake up the model
paras: The model is stuck because SFT only gives one signal: match the code string. But code strings are lossy descriptions of pictures. Two different strings render the same thing. So the model converges to a shallow pattern: memorize the most common code forms, ignoring nuance, because the text signal cannot tell the model that variant forms are equally valid—the model only sees that one form appears in the training data and copies it.

Introducing a visual judge adds a new channel of truth. Now the model gets feedback not just on string-matching but on picture correctness. This is harder to game. The model must genuinely understand which colors, values, and shapes to place where. Because the visual signal is independent of the code string, it pulls the model to richer, more accurate internal reasoning.

The two-stage curriculum matters: train with textual feedback first so the model learns syntax and data extraction in a stable way, because textual rules are clear and unambiguous—they give clear signals about which way to nudge the weights. Only then layer in visual feedback. If you mix them from the start, the model oscillates and struggles to converge, because the textual and visual signals pull in slightly different directions and the model cannot balance them. Training in stages is like learning to write first, then learning to make beautiful handwriting.

Code that is syntactically correct and visually similar

math.words: The total training signal is a weighted sum of three components: textual reward (for code correctness), visual reward (for picture similarity), and a regularization term to prevent the model from drifting too far from its starting point.
math.equation: R_total = w_text * R_text + w_visual * R_visual + beta * R_regularization

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a generated code receives R_text = 0.8 (code is mostly correct but one variable is wrong) and R_visual = 0.6 (chart shape is close but one bar is the wrong color).
The model learns that this code is pretty good (0.73 is high) but not perfect. In the next iteration, it tweaks both the variable and the color.
A second generated code gets R_text = 0.9 and R_visual = 0.9 (both judges agree this is excellent): R_total = 0.6 * 0.9 + 0.4 * 0.9 + 0.01 * 1.0 = 0.54 + 0.36 + 0.01 = 0.91.
The model strongly prefers the second code, so it learns to aim for dual correctness.

math.note: In words: the training signal combines textual correctness and visual fidelity, weighting each, so the model learns to write code that both parses and renders correctly, because high rewards encourage the model to explore code variations that satisfy both judges simultaneously.

charts.title: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone
charts.note: More training data does not help after this point; the curve plateaus, because the model has already learned the easy patterns that appear in most data, and new data just repeats those same patterns without revealing anything new.

charts.title: MSRL (multimodal SRL with text + visual)
charts.note: Both judges working together pull performance across all dimensions. The method beats the plateau by 6-10%.

items.b: Reward hacking on textual judge alone.
items.html: If you only optimize textual rewards (Stage 1 only), the model learns superficially: it writes syntactically correct code that passes basic checks but does not truly understand the chart. The visual judge catches this.

If you train with both textual and visual rewards from the start, gradients point in conflicting directions: text wants one kind of simplicity, visuals want another. The model oscillates and converges slowly. The paper shows this empirically; training in order (text first, then visual) is essential.

The visual reward model is trained on common charts. On rare or exotic chart types (uncommon combinations of stacked bars, rotated axes, unusual color schemes), it can give misleading scores. High-quality curation helps, because filtering examples to only the cleanest, most representative charts teaches both the main model and the visual reward model on the kinds of charts they will actually see.
Use real-world data for training (not synthetic), filter for high-quality examples, train stages in order, and pair both judges. The method works well across 24 different chart types.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small demo with a few real chart-code pairs. Train a simple model on them using only textual rewards until it plateaus (a few hundred iterations). Record the final accuracy (e.g., 65%). Then continue training with visual rewards for the same number of iterations. Plot the accuracy curves side-by-side. The visual-reward curve should climb above the textual plateau.
demo.closing: The one thing the demo must make impossible to miss: the model was stuck when judged by text alone, but visual feedback woke it up and pushed performance higher.
